items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.

items.title: A 1-in-300-million lottery ticket is almost always a bad investment
items.claim: Mega Millions: ~302 million possible combinations. A ticket costs $2. Jackpot of $600 million sounds like positive expected value (EV = 600M/302M = $2 — break even). But after taxes, lump sum discount, and ticket-splitting, real EV is well below $2.
items.prompt: How do you compute expected value correctly?

options.text: Sum over all outcomes of (probability * value). For a fair calculation, include ALL outcomes (not just the jackpot), tax adjustments, and the fact that big jackpots often have multiple winners who split the prize
Expected value is just the prize size

items.reveal:
Naive EV calculation for a lottery:
- Prize: $600M.
- Win probability: 1 / 302,000,000.
- EV from jackpot only: $600M / 302M ≈ $1.99.
- Ticket cost: $2.
- Naive net: -$0.01.

Real adjustments:
- Federal tax (~37% top bracket) plus state tax (variable, say 5%): take-home ~$330M instead of $600M.
- Lump sum vs annuity: lump sum is ~60% of advertised jackpot. Pre-tax lump sum: ~$360M. Post-tax: ~$200M.
- Jackpot splitting: when jackpots get large, more people play. Probability of multiple winners rises. Expected share is less than full jackpot.
- Other prizes: smaller wins (matching some numbers) contribute roughly $0.30 of EV per ticket. Better, but not enough.

Realistic EV: usually $0.50 - $1.00 per $2 ticket. Lottery is a regressive tax on the mathematically uninformed.

Linearity of expectation: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. A surprisingly powerful tool. The St. Petersburg paradox (already covered) is an exception where naive EV is infinite but psychological/practical value is finite.

Kelly criterion: optimal bet sizing when you have an edge. Even with positive EV, betting too much can lead to ruin. Bet fraction equals edge / odds. Most gamblers overbet, even when statistically lucky.

Applications:
- Insurance: companies sell policies with positive EV (for them); buyers accept negative EV in exchange for risk reduction.
- Investment decisions: long-run wealth is dominated by GEOMETRIC mean returns (Kelly).
- Game theory: mixed-strategy equilibria depend on equalising opponents' expected payoffs.
items.why: Expected value seems intuitive. Real computations require including hidden costs, taxes, and the structure of outcomes. The lottery survives because most players don't actually compute the math correctly — and because the entertainment value is real.
